newsitem.title: FRANCE: French political limbo seen if poll result is close.
newsitem.headline: French political limbo seen if poll result is close.

text.p: France could enter weeks of political limbo if voters elect a slim parliamentary majority on Sunday, preventing appointment of a cabinet until mid-June and passage of important laws until mid-July.

The rules under France's 1958 constitution could prove a major headache for France's next prime minister, tipped to be either Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin or centre-right National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin.

Under the rules, any parliamentarian named to the cabinet immediately loses the right to vote in parliament. New cabinet members then have a month of enforced reflection before formally ceding their seats to alternates elected on a joint ticket.
In recent elections, perhaps 20 deputies have been appointed to cabinet posts -- so a slim parliamentary majority would be instantly wiped out by their departure.

The constitution also states that the National Assembly's first session is on the second Thursday after the election -- June 12. The first session is devoted to electing a speaker, followed by key elections the next day of vice-presidents.
Needing a majority to pass these key votes, France's new prime minister might have to wait until June 14 to announce a cabinet.

Once the cabinet was in place, the government would then lose its parliamentary majority for the month's reflection for individual ministers. That in turn would prevent passage of any controversial legislation such as budget measures until July 14.

The rules were tested in 1967 and 1988 but there were fewer constraints because in both cases, a prime minister was already in place with defined policies -- Gaullist Georges Pompidou in 1967 and Socialist Michel Rocard in 1988.
Yet even Rocard, for instance, was only formally reappointed on the eve of the new National Assembly's first session. And his cabinet was only named five days after that.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe said on Monday he would stand down regardless of the outcome on Sunday after voters swung stunningly to the left on the first round on May 25, leaving a vacuum at the top of the ruling coalition.
